speaker: breeaclark
text: Good evening and welcome to tonight's City Council study session. We have two items on our agenda and the first is an update on the 36th Avenue Northwest Widening Project. I believe we have a presentation and I will turn it over to Mr. O'Leary, our Director

speaker: shawnoleary
text: of Public Works. Thank you, Mayor and Council. Appreciate that. Are you hearing me okay? Okay.

speaker: brendahall
text: I'm going to share my screen. I think I may have cut off the City Manager and he may have

speaker: darrelpyle
text: wanted to say something before we got started here. Not a problem, Madam Clerk. Just wanted to share this with Council. Bringing you this update as a result of a lot of telephone activity regarding 36th Avenue Northwest as it relates to or doesn't relate to our bond maintenance question on the ballot next Tuesday. Recognizing that construction projects like 36th Northwest are not a function of our road maintenance bond, but we did want to share with Council where this project sits and how quickly it can advance to construction should federal infrastructure dollars present themselves. So, Mr. O'Leary, please proceed.

speaker: shawnoleary
text: Thanks, sir. Appreciate that. Again, wanted to go back a little bit for Council, a little bit of background on the 2012 Transportation Bond Program. We are sensing we've been out talking to lots of groups about our Street Maintenance Bond Program election next Tuesday. And there does seem to be confusion among the citizens about the Transportation Bond election versus the Street Maintenance Bond election. So, we're going to talk here about the 2012 Transportation Bond election, which included eight major projects. And these are I refer to the term the capital T in Transportation as opposed to the little t in Maintenance. These are big projects. This is a big program. These tend to be road widening projects, a mile or two each. You can see where they were. Council worked for well over a year to develop this program. We went out and spoke to many, many groups before the election in August of 2012. And it had a really positive support of this program, $89 million program with about $42 million in bond funds. So, one of the reasons I think people vote for these bond elections here is we're getting more than a dollar back for our dollar of investment. So, I'll speak to that here in reference to this project. But we're getting more federal funds to build these projects than we're spending local bond funds. So, of the eight projects, six are complete and two are not. The two that are not are East Alameda Street, which we are getting ready to kick off construction this summer. So, that will be done quickly and perhaps even this construction season. That leaves us with the big one, 36th Avenue Northwest. That was always targeted as our last project in sequence. It is the second largest of the eight. It is a very expensive project, $17 million. And the scope of the project is only the second largest only to Lindsay Street. So, it just happened that we sequenced it as the last project. So, again, it is two miles of major road improvements starting at Tecumseh on the south and going to Indian Hills on the north. This is an old aerial map. But frankly, there hasn't been a ton more development in that area. When we were having this conversation with the community and the council back in 2012, final or preliminary class were coming in left and right in this area. But for whatever reason, many of them have not advanced to the final class stage for development. And some would suggest maybe that's because the road isn't done. But usually, it's the other first. Usually, development happens first. But anyway, this project is two miles of widening from two lanes to four lanes, two brand new major intersections, one at 36 and Franklin, the other one at 36 and Indian Hills. In addition to traffic signalization at those two locations, they will have multiple lanes, you know, double left turn lanes and all that sort of thing too. So, major, major road improvements. A fairly significant stormwater project here. This is Little River Basin. We have several channel crossings of the road. So, some, you know, pretty good size bridges in there or box culvert structures to build. And those are fairly expensive. Continuous sidewalks both sides and access to Ruby Grant Park. When we started this effort, we were hoping the road would get done before the park got done. And it's going to turn out to be the opposite, as you know. But we will finish Legacy Trail from Tecumseh up to Franklin and the entrance to Ruby Grant Park as part of this project. So, a 10-foot bike hike trail connecting to the one south of there along the project boundaries as well. And then, of course, the reason we have not started construction is because we do not have that federal funding match. These are two of the slides that we presented back in 2012. I think I met with, I felt like I met with 50 or 60 different groups and gave this presentation. But these are exactly out of that presentation that was made and endorsed by council and all of this done before the election in August of 2012. On the left side is a pretty number-rich slide. But this was the numbers that we were estimating for the program. So, again, an $89 million total investment in transportation and stormwater infrastructure with a $42 million investment of local bond funds and then seeking $46 million in federal transportation funds. You all saw a slide, an update slide on the 2012 bond program back in February as part of our capital budget retreat. And in just round numbers, I would tell you this program is probably coming in closer to $102,000 instead of $89,000. But we're also still coming in with about $54 million or $89 million, I'm going to say. We're also coming in with $54 million of federal funds if everything shakes out as we planned. So, we're still matching more than a dollar of federal funds for every dollar of local bond funds. So, again, this project was included in that 2012 program. The original budget included $11.5 million in federal funds. There seems to be some maybe confusion out there that somehow the numbers have changed. No, they haven't changed one bit. We have the $5,420,000 in the bank. Those are the bond funds that our local taxpayers have provided. But we don't have the $11.5 million in federal. That's the problem with this project. The federal funding limits and the rules and the ranking and rating have changed fairly dramatically in the last three years. But they were making subtle changes ever since we passed that bond election in 2012. So, in 2012, the maximum funding you could get for one project was $11.5 million. That's where that number came from. We knew we were eligible for up to $11.5 million for one project. So, that's what we put in the program. About two years later, ACOG changed the formula that we could acquire only $9.5 million for one project. So, we lost a couple million there. And then a few years after that, they reduced it down to $7.5 million. So, these changes in rules and the process with ACOG and federal funding has really impacted this project negatively. And that's, again, the problem that we're having here. The project originally scheduled for 2018 construction. So, we are now three years behind that schedule. And your staff drives us crazy that we're not delivering this project on schedule. We feel like we've come really close on the other projects, but this one is just kind of lingering on because we just don't have the funding to start work. Only the 36th Avenue Northwest and the East Alameda projects are not completed. And as I mentioned, East Alameda is all packaged up and going to construction this summer. So, that will leave 36th as the only one in that 2012 bond program that is not complete. And again, the city staff and the council began applying for those federal funds back in federal fiscal 2017. It was actually calendar 2016, right on schedule. So, we knew we were seeking those 2017-2018 funds, but we have failed to get that grant for now six consecutive years. So, here's where we are today. We are really, Darrell asked me, and I believe the right term is shovel ready. We really are. There's a lot of details in the design process and so on as we deal with ODOT and the federal funding scheme. So, technically speaking, the engineering plans are 90% on phase one. We've broken this up into two phases. Again, just like we did 24th Avenue East, we had to break the project up into two different funding years in order to fund the whole project. So, we're planning to do the same thing here with 36 because the maximum is now 7.5 million in one year. So, phase one is that southern mile that comes to the Franklin. Phase two is the northern mile, Franklin to Indian Hills. 90% complete on the plans on phase one, 75% complete on phase two. We can get to completion very quickly once we know that we have the federal funds acquired or some funds acquired for the project. All the land is acquired for phase one. We're having a little challenge in phase two, that northern phase. We've got about 10 property owners who are not willing to negotiate voluntarily. So, council has recently approved a eminent domain resolution, and we are actively, our legal team is actively pursuing that process. Among those 10 property owners are two of the developers in the area. And then, utilities, we're down to one, a couple of poles for Western Farmers Electric Co-op there in that southern mile. Getting real close again, that worked out. So, we're really ready on phase one. And then, those utility relocations depend on that right of way in phase two. So, we're kind of stuck here. We had fully intended to get that right of way on that northern mile sooner, but I didn't expect to have 10 folks holding out on us. Again, city matching funds are currently in the bank. That $5.4 million is in the bank, just like we promised back in 2012. We just don't have the $11.5 million in federal funds to match it. And then, as you know, the scoring process and ranking and rating process at ACOG has changed pretty dramatically. And as I mentioned earlier, we just have not been able to get this project to rank adequately for the funding through the normal ACOG funding process. That's why the project is stopped and not moving forward to construction. So, I think what Daryl wanted us to discuss tonight was, how else can we accomplish this project? It's certainly not a problem with having it ready to go and ready to start construction. It is simply a funding problem, but the number is big. It's $11.5 million. That's a very large number for any of our budgets. So, it's going to have to come from some other large source. As you know, there are two federal funding plans currently bouncing around. One that has been approved by Congress called the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, which is pretty much COVID-19 related. And Daryl can provide some updates on where those funds are, and they're moving their way into Norman for sure. The other bill that is out there bouncing around, and we think there might be some movement even as early as tomorrow in Congress, is called Build Back Better. It's the infrastructure plan that we've been hearing about, frankly, for, oh goodness, I've been involved in that discussion for five or six years, and just hasn't been able to work its way out of Congress. But there seems to be new momentum, and it's a large proposal, and it's infrastructure, so it fits this project very well. We hope. We don't know the rules or the red tape yet, but that could be another source for this $11.5 million. So, if we can find that money, the design can be complete in June, no later than June. We think we can get through that eminent domain process by June this year as well. Utilities will be probably done simultaneous to construction. Usually they're out ahead of the road construction, but we can do them simultaneously. That means we could bid both projects, we think, by August. We could even bid phase one earlier if we have the funding, and then we could begin construction on the entire two miles no later than October of this year, if we have the funding. So, just wanted to leave it there, and Daryl might have some additional comments about those federal funding opportunities.
